sourceInformation.genre: Surgical action (arcade operation game) with a visual-novel story
sourceInformation.perspective: First-person surgeon's-eye 3D operative field; staged third-person story scenes
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js r180 (WebGPU, WebGL2 fallback), TSL ink post-filter, Rapier 0.19.3, Web Audio, Gamepad API, esbuild 0.28.2; hub session client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: Comic-book medical drama: cel-shaded toon materials, ink outline filter, manga tone, all geometry made in code
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer with code-built clips, skinned strains, procedural follow-through
sourceInformation.audio: All synthesized in code: step-sequenced music, procedural effects, Animalese-style gibberish voices; music at 10% by default
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, shared world, 1–4 players; couch co-op on its own
sourceInformation.testing: Headless sim suite 51 checks, Playwright browser suite 80 checks on Chromium and WebKit, hub harness 26 checks. No physical controller, no second human, no real iOS device.
sourceInformation.research: AI Hub protocol and harness, engine prototypes on this computer, and the plan's notes on the source.

testingFeedback: The sim suite (51 checks) and the hub harness (26 checks) caught the issues that would have shipped. The browser suite (80 checks) caught UI timing: attract was swallowing the next confirm, and a reload was dropping screens the playthrough had already opened.
A few were critical: a story line that failed the Bea lint, snapshot traffic that could trip the hub rate warning, and a ready() call that the client ignores if it happens before welcome.
The most helpful test was the Normal bot playthrough with the 45 to 75 percent clear-time band. It kept the operations honest.
The least helpful test was staring at a single still of the title. Behavior checks found the breaks. A picture did not.
engineFeedback: MeshToonNodeMaterial plus the ink graph is a complete look from primitives, and the hub client is small enough to read.
WebGPU on this machine needs five browser flags or the device dies after one frame. Rapier must be initialized before the first world, and ready() is a no-op until the welcome arrives.
The operation sim, the bot, and the snapshot codec. The engine draws and hears. It does not know surgery.
Software WebGPU is slow enough that a test has to drive the sim with step and warp, and four inked views in one harness is a memory tightrope.
Nothing in the engine source. The operative rules live in this game.
A supported way to boot SwiftShader WebGPU without a private flag recipe, and a ready() that queues until welcome instead of vanishing.
promptFeedback: The plan is specific about feel: ten-foot type, one patient, four surgeons, and a story that knows when to be quiet.
Two WebGPU flag lists disagree. The shorter one draws a blank here. The plan's five flags are the ones that work.
Keeping a sloppy four-surgeon coda inside the rules without moving the Normal scores, then proving the hub harness on software WebGPU.
Say once, in the prompt, which browser flags this computer actually needs.

aiHub.name: Alive in Common Time
aiHub.description: A rain-soaked surgical melodrama at St. Alder. Cut, clamp and keep time with an engineered parasite while the head nurse judges your hands. One to four surgeons, one patient.
aiHub.controls: Right stick or mouse to aim, left stick or 1-8 for tools, R2 or left click to use
